typed_animation_stream.note: Mixed WORD/LONG source stream supports frame refs, REPEAT, SETMODE, velocity LONG operands/modes, PAUSE, SETSPEED, zero velocities, facing/xflip and END. Unknown commands stop explicitly. ANI_REPEAT was executing as ANI_END -- both shared a case in the interpreter and it set ended=true. ANIM.ASM:364 _ani_repeat rewinds OANIPC to OANIBASE and jumps to _next_command1: it is a loop. 169 of the 1,525 emitted programs contain one, including every idle stance and every torso cycle, and all of them died after a single pass. Fixed to rewind to the program's `entry` (not op 0 -- change_anim1a writes the routine's own address into OANIBASE, so a program whose stream begins with shared code it branches back into rewinds to its own first command). The flat wm_visual track beside the VM had always handled repeat correctly, so the two implementations disagreed and the one Bret's display uses was the right one. ANI_IFROPE and ANI_IFNOTROPE were emitted with no branch destination. The emitter registered the fixup and resolved the label correctly, then _c_op wrote -1 because it only reads op[1] as a target for ops listed in BRANCH_OPS and those two were not in it -- 75 branches in all. In the interpreter (size_t)-1 fails the dispatch loop's `pc < op_count` test and falls straight out into ended=true, so a wrestler within 100 of a rope did not fall back: his animation stopped before its first frame. Seven programs, every wrestler's break_neck among them. Both halves are fixed -- the two ops are in BRANCH_OPS, and a branch whose target is negative now falls through rather than ending the animation -- and two source-tool tests guard it: no emitted branch may carry a negative target, and any op that registers a fixup must be listed in BRANCH_OPS. The whole corpus is now played by a test rather than sampled: tests/arcade_port/anim/test_corpus.c starts every emitted program with the physics running -- wrestler_veladd then wrestler_friction then the animation tick, WRESTLE.ASM:2457's own order -- ticks each for 400 ticks, and follows the ANI_CHANGEANIM hand-offs the way wrestler_backend.c:196 does, because ANI_CHANGEANIM replaces an animation rather than stopping it. Both halves are load-bearing: without an integrator nineteen programs never show a frame, every one of them parked on ANI_WAITHITGND waiting for a landing nothing was producing; without following the hand-offs, every routine that opens with one reads as frameless. With both, exactly one program in the game holds frame ops it never shows -- bam_roll_frames, a roll-frame data table the emitter reads as a program and nothing ever starts -- and the test asserts that list exactly, so a second one and a fix to this one both fail. Playing everything found two more defects of the ANI_IFROPE shape. First, 1,794 label entries named an op index one past their program's last op: a routine's trailing assembly, its puppet table and its `equ` lines all sit after the last animation command (BAMSEQ2.ASM's `#yoff equ 50` after bam_4_losebal_anim's ANI_END is the plainest case), and each symbol among them was recorded at index len(ops). Nothing at the C end tells that apart from a real index, so wm_anim_program_label answered an ANIPC redirect to `#yoff` or `#puppet_tbl` with a position the dispatcher reads as "the program is over". The emitter now keeps only labels that name a reachable op and refuses to emit a branch resolving past the end. Second, ANIM.ASM:29 implements ANI_IFSTATUS as a raw write to the animation PC (`move a0,a4`), so a routine may branch to any address -- including the head of a later routine, spelled `SUBR name`. wlanim.label_def cannot see that (its GLOBAL_LABEL_RE wants the name alone in column 0, which is what it needs for the other job it does, delimiting a local label's scope), so program_for could not find the definition and refused bam_faceup_getup_anim, dnk_faceup_getup_anim and yok_combo_scissor_anim outright. ANI_CHANGEANIM elsewhere names all three, so a wrestler knocked onto his back changed to an animation nothing had emitted and stopped where he lay. Branch resolution now counts a SUBR line as a definition: the corpus went from 1,525 programs to 1,530, four more real frames appeared in frame_geometry, and and the dangling ANI_CHANGEANIM set went from 54 operands over five labels to two. Those last two were not dangling in the arcade build, as first recorded here: DNKSEQ2.ASM defines dnk_combo_hammer_anim (:3031) and re_enter_combo_hiptoss (:4429) as bare column-0 labels rather than SUBRs, and the roster pass enumerates SUBR lines, so both were emitted by nothing while an ANI_CHANGEANIM further down the same file named each. wlpuppet.changeanim_op_targets now reads the plain op the way its siblings read ANI_SLAVEANIM's and ANI_CHANGEANIM_TBL's tables; the corpus is 1,532 programs and the test asserts that no ANI_CHANGEANIM operand goes unresolved at all. The programs that never end are accounted for too, rather than left as a count: 292 are still running after 400 ticks, and a count alone cannot tell a genuine idle stance from one wedged on a condition that will never come true. The test records every frame each one shows and requires it to show one twice -- a program revisiting a frame it already played is cycling by observation. 291 of the 292 do. The one that does not is WRESTLE2.ASM:3992 xxx_dead_anim, which ends on ANI_ROT ("just sit and do nothing", ANIM.ASM:4441): it holds the frame that is showing, which is how a dead wrestler stays down, and started cold there is no frame to hold. Each wrestler's OWN turn, walk and torso animation tables are now generated for the whole roster (tools/wlwrestlertbl.py -> src/generated/wrestler_anim_tables.c), the other half of the per-wrestler animation data beside wlrostertbl.py's global WRESTLERNUM-indexed tables. WRESTLE.ASM reaches three per wrestler through its own dispatch lists (:5031 torso, :5043 legs, :5100 rotate), and all three are read from those lists rather than built from a prefix: slot 7 is Adam Bomb, cut from the game, and carries Doink's tables, while the Referee's rotate slot is a plain 0. The defining file is resolved against WRESTLE.CMD because DNK.ASM and DOINK.ASM both define dnk_rotate_anims_table and TEMPLATE.ASM holds a copy of bam_rotate_anims_table -- only DOINK.ASM and BAM.ASM are linked. Shapes are the index arithmetic in change_walk_anim, not a choice: `srl 1` then `X4` gives the 4x4 diagonal-only turn matrices, `X8` unshifted the 8x8 full-compass leg table, and a table that does not fill its shape is refused rather than padded. 27 tables, 864 label slots, every one of them naming a program the port already emits. Bret's and Razor's three were in the port already, transcribed by hand into src/core/arcade/wm_arcade_{bret,razor}_tables.c. The generated data was compared against both before either was removed and all 192 labels matched, so the hand transcription is confirmed correct and those two files are retired rather than left as a second copy that can drift. The point of having them is WRESTLE.ASM:4946 change_walk_anim and :5062 set_rotate_anim, now translated in the shared program backend (wm_wrestler_backend_execute_walk). Until this, that backend called wm_execute_walk and nothing else: the seven wrestlers who use it never reselected a leg animation while walking, never played a turn when their facing changed, and left the second animation channel frozen on whatever *_ani_init started it with. The structure follows the source, including which half runs when -- change_walk_anim is reached only from the eight real-movement walk_table handlers and never from #zip, so both its halves sit under MOVE_DIR != 0, and set_rotate_anim reads FACING_DIR as it was before wm_execute_walk's WM_MOVE_ZIP catch-up. One approximation is carried over rather than papered over: the source gates the torso half on ANIMODE2, the second channel's mode word, and this port has a single anim_mode on the actor with nothing writing an ANIMODE2, so the gate is the primary channel's -- the same approximation Bret's hand-built backend has always made. Splitting ANIMODE2 out is its own change. The per-wrestler work is finished with the fourth table and the routines behind it. WRESTLE2.ASM:4079 #special_moves gives each wrestler an smove table -- the secret-move monitor processes init_smoves spawns at match start -- and every one of the eight wraps its finishing-move entries in `.if NUM_<name>_FINISHES`. GAME.EQU:580-587 sets seven of those switches to 0 and Undertaker's `> 1` guard excludes his second, so the shipped game has exactly ONE finishing move, und_finish_move1, and the other fifteen *_finish_move routines were skipped along with their table entries (their SUBR definitions sit inside the same `.if` blocks). The port's eight hand-written copies of these tables carried eleven of them between them; all eight are now read with the conditions honoured, a source-tool test holds each in-tree copy to the generated table, and the two Bret/Razor finishing-move monitors that were fully translated are kept and labelled as cut content rather than deleted -- the smove table no longer lists either, which is what decides whether the game can reach them. tools/port_coverage.py learned the same thing: a SUBR inside a `.if` the assembler evaluated as false is not an untranslated routine, it is a routine that never shipped, and counting it as open inflates the denominator with work that does not exist. 77 routines in the linked source are like that -- 30 under `.if DEBUG` (SYS.EQU:13 sets it to 0), 30 finishing moves, 16 under a plain `.if 0`, and one under `.if NMBPAL`. A condition the tool cannot decide leaves the routine counted, so an unreadable `.if` can only make coverage look worse than it is. und_finish_move1 itself is translated (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_und_finish.h) with its two helpers adjust_view and shake_world: all seven guards read off the source (opponent MODE_DEAD, second pin attempt, not a drone, inside the ring, has not already pinned him, and NEITHER wrestler right of RING_X_CENTER+100 because the coffin comes in from the left), the buckoff bits, the 32-step scroll to the midpoint, and the shaker's jitter about a fixed origin. DOINK.ASM:1594 do_taunt is translated too, with its #taunt_t table: a human taunts only while holding UP and BLOCK, a drone on an RNDPER(250) draw. All eight wrestler files are now fully accounted for; 2043 of 2534 routines overall. The animation finally has a route to a screen. The N64 platform layer and the ported game were two different programs: src/platform/n64/main.c drew wm_demo_fighter through a wm_visual_sequence track and never named wm_arcade_actor_t, wm_anim_exec or wm_wrestler_backend once, and its match renderer was switched off deliberately ("the existing combat renderer is a development harness only"), so none of the translated animation reached a frame buffer. wm/match_display.h is the seam, and it is in the portable core rather than the platform because the platform cannot be compiled without libdragon and therefore cannot be tested: draw ORDER, which layers exist, and where the torso hangs off the body are all game logic with exact answers in the source. Order is DISPLAY.ASM:1248 obj_yzsort's -- ascending Z, then ascending Y within equal Z -- where the demo renderer compared screen Y alone, which is neither key. The torso layer is gated on the body frame's channel-2 attachment pair, now carried in frame geometry for all 5,126 roster frames (748 have one). What this deliberately does NOT do is project world coordinates onto the screen: the source scrolls a world through WORLDTLX/WORLDTLY, the port has no translated projection, and inventing one would be a guess dressed as a translation -- items carry the actor's own world position and placing it stays the platform's job until obj_addworldxy and friends are translated.

source_dependency_ir.note: CI scans every SUBR/SUBRP and static CALL/JSRP/CREATE edge and emits dependency frontiers for attract_mode and start_match without inventing unresolved dynamic semantics.

animation_source_ir.note: CI scans typed WORD/LONG animation data and W/L packing macros across the original ASM tree, preserving source expressions and unresolved forms without inventing pointer or command semantics.

text_engine.note: STRING.ASM's whole text engine is translated (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_string.h): the two 80-character message buffers, ADJUST.ASM:1593 BINBCD, dec_to_asc (seven digits, leading zeros suppressed, the clamp's cmp/jrhi polarity kept) and dec_to_pct, copy/concat for both buffers and for ROM strings, get_string_len2's per-line pixel measurement including its trailing -mess_spacing, the three justification hooks plus setup_message's no-op one, and print_string2b's cursor walk with its in-band newline (code 1) that re-justifies every line on its own width. All ten live *_ascii font tables are extracted by tools/wlstring.py into src/generated/font_tables.c (128 slots each; the commented-out sgmd8_ascii is not emitted). Glyph widths are real: STRING.ASM does not hold them (the printer reads the image header's first word at run time), so the same tool measures them out of the shipped IMG/*.IMG WIMP containers into src/generated/font_metrics.c -- 280 of the 375 symbols the tables name, covering every letter and digit of every font. The other 95 are named in that file and left to a width seam rather than invented: 46 are stored under an eight-character name another symbol shares and need FONTS.LOD's packing order to separate (that file is zero bytes in this tree), and the 49 osgmd10_* glyphs have no artwork in any container here. Drawing itself -- the arcade's BEGINOBJP -- is a seam.

palette_allocator.note: PAL.ASM's allocator is translated (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_pal.h) against SYS.EQU's TUNIT constants -- NUMPAL/NMFPAL 80, NMBPAL 0, NUMPALT 60, PAL64 0: pal_init (including taking DIAGP as colour map 0), pal_find, pal_getf, pal_set, pal_transfer, pal_clean, pal_blacken, pal_fade, pal_addb and all four do_fade entry points. Counting external call sites is what set the scope: pal_getf has 76 callers, pal_clean 20, fade_down 17, fade_up 13, pal_find 5, pal_set 5, pal_init 3, pal_transfer 1, fade_down_half 1 -- and pal_blacken, pal_fadein, pal_fadeout, pal_fadeout2, pal_fadeinx, pal_fadeoutx, pal_fmwht, pal_towht, addbrt_ae and fade_up_half have none at all. The process wrappers in that dead half are not translated; pal_fade and pal_addb, which are what they drive, are. pal_getb is not translated because it is not assembled: it sits inside `.if NMBPAL` and so does its one caller (BAKGND.ASM:632), which falls through to pal_getf. 396 palettes are extracted whole by tools/wlpal.py into src/generated/palettes.c, count word included -- IMGPAL.ASM's 337 plus WRESPAL.ASM's 59 alternate-colour ones. WRESTLE.CMD links both files and they share names, so the extractor honours `.if`: seven of WRESPAL.ASM's palettes (BAMBLU_P, DNKBLU_P, LEXWHT_P, RZRGRN_P, SHNRED_P, UNDPRP_P, YOKRED_P) sit inside `.if 0` and each has a live counterpart in IMGPAL.ASM, and UNDGRN_P and UNDBLU_P are two labels stacked on one block and share it. and wm_pal_getf_by_name is the bridge for the animation VM's pal_getf seam. Two seams remain: pal_clean's OBJLST/BAKLST walk arrives as an in_use question, and pal_transfer writes into an ordinary array indexed exactly as the source computes the COLRAM address rather than into hardware.

award_conditions_and_powerups.note: AWARD.ASM's icon accounting was already ported (wm/award.h); the routines that decide whether an award is earned were not, and are now: is_it_a_really_quick_win, give_award_if_opponent_is_human, arm_comeback_award / check_for_award_for_big_comeback, and get_num_awards. Two shipped quirks came with them and are reproduced rather than repaired. is_it_a_really_quick_win's `cmpi 69 / jrgt / jruc` makes its SUPER_QUICK and VERY_QUICK branches unreachable (both are worth zero icons, so the game is unaffected). rst_awards clears (NUM_AWARDS*2)-1 bytes -- sixty-three -- from p1rnd_award, running into the adjacent p2rnd_award and stopping one short of its end, so player 2's award-31 round slot is never reset; award 31 is unused. The whole powerup system is new (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_powerup.h): the eight button codes, PUPWAITSWITCH's state machine and get_powerups' reconciliation. PUPWAITSWITCH has three properties worth stating: the first press has no deadline (`clr a11` then `dec` wraps), every press after it shares one TSEC*2 budget that is never reset, and a wrong press costs a tick rather than restarting the code. Two codes are not what they look like: drone_meters has no sequence at all (its PUPWAITSWITCHes are commented out, so it turns itself on in a one-player one-on-one match), and no_ring has a complete four-step sequence but is never spawned -- its CREATE is commented out, 'Disable until we get blimp module'. These flags are what wm_arcade_mode_dead.h's instant_combos_on, wm_arcade_combat.h's hyper_speed_on and wm_arcade_lifebar.h's move-names toggle had been naming as absent. The display half of AWARD.ASM -- icon bars, dufus message boxes, the MK3 tip screen, the sparkle -- is still object drawing and is not translated.

cabinet_switch_word.note: MAIN.ASM's 64-bit switch latch and everything that reads it are translated (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_switches.h): the current/previous/newly-pressed/newly-released derivation at MAIN.ASM:811, WRESTLE2.ASM's per-player slicing (get_stick_val_cur/down/up, get_but_val_cur/down/up), UTIL.ASM's get_start_cur/down and all ten aggregators, the #xflip_table that turns an absolute stick reading into a facing-relative one, and read_switches' per-wrestler caching including its immobilize clear and both STICK_REL derivations. The latch is modelled as one 64-bit word because the reads require it: `but_offs2` is `20h-3`, so a player's high two buttons are a sixteen-bit field starting at bit 0x1D masked to bits 3 and 4 -- latch bits 0x20 and 0x21, across the halfway line. A 32-bit model would silently lose block and super punch. wm/human_input.h's direct N64-pad mapping remains the live path and still documents itself as a simplification; this module is the real one for the code that needs it, starting with the AWARD.ASM powerup codes. Two details recorded rather than smoothed: read_switches derives STICK_REL_CUR from FACING_DIR's PLAYER_RIGHT_BIT while the standalone wres_get_stick_rel_cur tests the sprite's FLIPH bit for the same purpose, and the immobilize test is `jrp` -- strictly positive, so a zero timer does not freeze anyone. What is not here is the hardware end: FSWITCH itself, and MAIN.ASM's inversion of the raw read, arrive as the caller's uint64_t.

roster_predicates.note: WRESTLE2.ASM's roster predicates (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_teammates.h): ck_teammate_pin, ck_live_teammates, ck_any_teammates, is_a14_behind and clr_climb. The first three share a preamble -- skip empty slots, skip yourself, skip the other side -- and differ only in the single test at the end, so they stay three functions here rather than one with a mode argument. ck_live_teammates is what wm_arcade_combat.h's victim_has_live_teammates seam had been asking for. Two details are the source's: is_a14_behind subtracts and branches on sign, so an opponent at exactly the same X counts as being on the left (`jrn` needs a strictly negative difference), and clr_climb sets SAFE_TIME to 1 rather than 0 -- `clr a0 / move / inc a0 / move` -- giving one tick of grace so the wrestler is not immediately re-caught by whatever he just climbed out of. idiot_check was already ported in wmania_ring_climb; update_timer and wrestler_counter are object drawing and are not here.

shared_rand.note: The arcade has one @RAND and one RNDRNG0 (UTIL.ASM:1713), and every caller in the game stirs the same state. src/core/pregame.c and src/core/select_screen.c each carried a local xorshift instead, on the stated grounds that RNDRNG0 was 'external/shared Wolf Unit code ... not present in this game's source drop' and 'not present in the checked-in WWF source tree'. Both claims were wrong: the routine is in UTIL.ASM and this port already had it translated as wm_rng_rndrng0. Both now take a WmRng * and app.c hands them the same &app->rng the match uses, so the ladder shuffle, the scramble and the random-select cursor all draw from one stream, as the source does. A NULL or unstirred WmRng makes every draw zero -- that is the arcade's own behaviour (RAND is stirred only by HCOUNT and the stack pointer) and the ladder inherits it visibly: with no shuffle the opponents come out 7, 6, 5, 4 in INIT_TEMP_TABLE order. There is a test for that case as well as for the driven one.

absence_claims_audit.note: A sweep of every place this port claimed a routine was missing from the source tree. Four claims existed; three were false. RNDRNG0 is UTIL.ASM:1713 (pregame.c and select_screen.c both said otherwise and each carried a local xorshift). INSBOBJ is DISPLAY.ASM:1540 and obj_yzsort is DISPLAY.ASM:1248 (bmod.h said the shared body was 'not present in this game's source drop' and described its ordering as matched to observed output). The reconstruction happened to be right -- INSBOBJ's own header says 'List is sorted by increasing z and increasing y within constant z' and obj_yzsort's equal-Z test is `jrge`, so exact ties are stable -- but it is now cited rather than inferred, with a test. One claim was true: hrt_2_super_punch_anim really does not exist; only hrt_4_super_punch_anim (HRTSEQ2.ASM:223) does. Separately, wm_arcade_closest.c used a textbook integer square root where WRESTLE.ASM:4183 calls SQUARE.ASM's square_root, on the argument that only the exact closest_xdist/closest_zdist fields gate behaviour. That argument has since stopped holding -- wm_arcade_drone.c compares closest_dist against 200 and wm_arcade_doink.c against 0x70 -- so the arcade's deliberately quantised table lookup is what decides those now.

life_data_table.note: LIFEBAR.ASM's life_data table (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_life_data.h): PLT_LIFE, PLT_CLIFE, PLT_TURBO and PLT_COMBO_SIZE per wrestler, the three resets, inc_life and get_health. The port already had adjust_health and an actor life field; PLT_CLIFE -- the *displayed* life, which chases the real one at `#lifebar_deltavee equ 2` pixels a tick -- was missing, and it is what makes the bar drain smoothly rather than snap. The three resets disagree in ways that show on screen and each has a test: init_life_data leaves CLIFE at ZERO while LIFE is already full, so the bars visibly fill up over 81 ticks at the start of a match; init_wres_life_data snaps CLIFE to full instead, because a change_wrestler swap is replacing someone who just died and there is nothing to animate; and init_rnd_life_data writes LIFE and CLIFE only, deliberately leaving combo_size and turbo alone where the other two clear them. clear_lifebar zeroes PLT_LIFE alone, so the bar drains to meet it. PLT_TURBO is written by two of the three resets and read by nothing anywhere in the source -- there is no turbo bar in this game -- and that is asserted rather than left as a comment. The meter objects, the flashing processes and the credit box (meters, SET_FLASHING, rewire_meter, draw_combo_meter) are object drawing and are not translated.

roster_animation_tables.note: The eighteen global per-wrestler animation tables (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_roster_anims.h, extracted by tools/wlrostertbl.py). These are the 'everyone does this, each in his own animation' tables the source indexes by WRESTLERNUM: fall_back_tbl, fall_back_tbukl_tbl, body_hit2_tbl, hitblock_tbl, hitonground_tbl, the six climb tables in WRESTLE2.ASM, FINISEQ.ASM's stand_table and dizzy_table, and the rest. tools/wlpuppet.py already resolved the tables named as command operands (ANI_SLAVEANIM, ANI_CHANGEANIM_TBL) from their use sites, because those labels are #local and reused; these are the plain globals reached by ordinary code, one definition each. Labels defined more than once (SLAM_HIM, flyout_tbl) are refused here and left to wlpuppet. Slot 7 is Adam Bomb, cut from the game, and slot 9 the Referee, present only in the tables that declared ten rows -- the row count and the contents are two separate statements, so the six climb tables give both slots Doink's animation while hitonground_tbl declares ten rows and leaves both empty. The detail that shows the data had to be read rather than derived: fall_back_tbukl_tbl points Yokozuna at yok_fall_back_anim where every other wrestler gets his own *_fall_back_tbukl_anim, and yok_fall_back_tbukl_anim is not a routine anywhere in the source. A source-tool test checks every label in every table against the real SUBR list, so a generator that derived rows from the prefix would fail it.

secondary_animation_channel.note: ANIM.ASM's second animation channel -- ANIBASE2/ANIPC2/ANIMODE2/ANICNT2, driven by change_anim2 and change_anim2a. It is the torso, and every wrestler has one: each *_ani_init starts a stand animation on channel 1 and a torso animation on channel 2, chosen by FACING_DIR's PLAYER_RIGHT_BIT. Bret's hand-built backend has had a second visual track since it was written; the shared backend the other seven use had none, so seven of the eight wrestlers ran with no torso at all. wm_wrestler_backend_actor now carries a torso_prog beside prog and ticks both, and wm_wrestler_backend_ani_init translates the shared *_ani_init from tools/wlaniinit.py's extracted label table (nine slots; slot 7 is Adam Bomb and is empty). All four change_anim entry points are now named for what they are: the guarded forms carry change_anim1/2's already-playing check, and starting a SECONDARY animation deliberately does not reset gravity where a primary one does -- the torso does not fall. What is still missing is the drawing: the torso frame is published by wm_wrestler_backend_torso_frame and nothing composites it.

undertaker_coffin_finish.note: FINISEQ.ASM's coffin sequence is the only finishing move the assembler built (GAME.EQU:580-587 sets NUM_TAKER_FINISHES to 1 and the other seven to 0), and it is now translated down to its last decision (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_coffin.h). The sequence is three processes and one animation talking through four globals, and the split here is between what they DECIDE and what they DRAW. Decided, and translated: the @close_the_door / @close_the_floor / @guy_in / @guy_up handshake and all four of its polls; set_speeds, whose Z half snaps a wrestler standing behind WRES_Z onto it and then computes the velocity from the snapped value, so it comes out zero and he teleports the distance in one tick; the coffin's rise and fall ramps, the rise testing OSIZEY against 136 for EQUALITY and the fall for <= 1; hover_coffin's bob, whose turnaround is `movk 1,a8 / not a8` -- a ones complement, so the up delta is -2 and not the -1 the comment beside it claims, and only the +/- turn fires its eight puffs of smoke; the door-slam shake, whose X jitter is -2..+2 but whose Y jitter is RNDRNG0(2)-2, so the coffin only ever jumps upward; and ltl_exp's six RNDRNG0 draws in the source's own order, because they come off one shared stream. Drawn, and ledgered rather than invented: the BEGINOBJ/obj_aniq/DELOBJA8 choreography. The frame lists keep the source's own image names and their SHAPE, which is where the surprises are: #mat_anim2 and #cof_anim2 are not animations at all but bare `.long 0` terminators the closing loops walk BACKWARDS from with `move *-a9`, so closing plays the opening frames in reverse and there is no second list; and #tstone_anim is dead, because und_coffin_up:668 has `movi #tstone_anim,a9` commented out in favour of #tstone_test, which begins one frame later -- the shipped tombstone skips TMBSTN01. Two gaps in the tooling had hidden real work. disappear_wrestler -- the animation that makes the dead man vanish once the door shuts -- was emitted by nothing: every discovery rule keyed on an `_anim` suffix and this is the one animation in the game without one, so the sequence's last step pointed at a program that did not exist. wlprogram now also follows a `movi <label>,aN` that reaches a `calla change_anim1a` within five lines, which is a stronger signal than the naming convention rather than a weaker one; across every linked file it finds exactly that one label. And stand_wrestler/dizzy_wrestler index two per-wrestler FACETBLs written as ` SUBRP stand_table` rather than as column-0 labels, so wlpuppet's table reader could not see them; it now accepts either spelling and reads both, eighteen rows out of the source instead of transcribed. Those two routines call change_anim1a on a13 ITSELF, which ANIPC cannot express -- the target is not a label in any program the caller is running -- so the actor carries a change_anim_label the VM turns into a hand-off and clears the moment the routine returns.

special_move_watchdogs.note: WRESTLE2.ASM:4058 init_smoves is the process spawner every wrestler's secret moves hang off: once per MATCH, one SMOVE_PID watchdog per entry in his smove table. Nothing in this port called it, and the consequence was not just missing moves -- und_finish_move1 is an entry in und_smove_table and is reached by nothing else, so the Undertaker's coffin finish was unreachable however completely FINISEQ.ASM was translated. Now translated end to end (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_smove.h): init_smoves, reset_smoves (WRESTLE.ASM:6141), kill_smove_procs (WRESTLE2.ASM:3896), and MACROS.H:652 WAITSWITCH_DWN, which every one of these monitors is built from and whose five behaviours are all load-bearing -- it compares `(BUT_VAL_DOWN << 4) | STICK_REL_NEW`, so a direction counts once and only relative to facing; it FAILS on the wrong input rather than ignoring it, the opposite of AWARD.ASM's PUPWAITSWITCH; it fails outright while SPECIAL_MOVE_ADDR is set; its countdown is decremented BEFORE the test, so the `clr a11` every monitor opens with wraps to -1 and gives the first input no deadline at all; and the one `movi #TIMEOUT,a11` after that is SHARED by every remaining step rather than reset per step. Three of the 65 distinct monitors are implemented and the other 62 are a counted gap rather than a silent one: every one is a bare column-0 label rather than a SUBR, so tools/port_coverage.py -- which enumerates SUBR lines -- never had them in its denominator at all, and a source-tool test now holds the registry to the tables and the count to 62. The three are und_finish_move1 (UP, DOWN, PUNCH, then the seven guards already translated), and std_walk_fast and std_taunt, which every wrestler carries: both a full eight-way clockwise stick rotation sharing one 61-tick budget, one starting at AWAY and one at UP with B_BLOCK masked out of every step. Two things had to be built to reach them. STICK_REL_CUR/STICK_REL_NEW -- read_switches' last two derivations, which nothing in this port computed, so the relative stick every WAITSWITCH_DWN reads was always zero. And the pin: WRESTLE2.ASM:3925 can_pin is a callback all eight dispatchers already call and NOTHING ever supplied, so no wrestler in this port could pin anybody. It is now translated -- the other-team live/zombie sweep, the 70h/50h range pair, the B_PINABLE test, and the five side effects that make it an act rather than a predicate (PINNED, WHOPINNEDME, three velocities zeroed, the KOD clear) -- and supplied by both backends. With it, AWARD.ASM:1768 pin_prompt's decision half moves @p1pins/@p2pins on the tick a side is wiped out, which is the count und_finish_move1 gates on. The sequence then has to FINISH: ANI_CREATEPROC had a seam and no implementation, so und_coffin_up and raise_dead never ran, @finish_completed was never set, TAKER.ASM:697's #fdone_wait spun forever, and @in_finish_move would have stayed raised for the rest of the match with the scroller frozen and the round never called. Both now run: raise_dead is its own three lines, and und_coffin_up/do_up_coffin/hover_coffin are a state machine over the source's own sleeps that moves the four globals at the points the source moves them. The camera (WRESTLE2.ASM:1681 scroll_world) is wired at the same time, because adjust_view writes @WORLDTLX and the scroller's own gate is @in_finish_move. A live-match test drives the whole chain: start a match as the Undertaker, set up the guards, press UP-DOWN-PUNCH, and watch the dead man stand, the coffin rise, the door open and shut, the tombstone come up and @in_finish_move clear. What is still NOT here: the 62 other monitors, and every object the sequence would draw -- the count of ltl_exp smoke puffs each tick is carried for a renderer, but nothing makes them. SINCE: 42 more monitors are translated, taking the implemented count from 3 of 65 to 45 and the gap from 62 to 20. They were not written out. 42 of the 62 are ONE routine written out 42 times with different constants -- the head-hold family, whose shape is a MODE_HEADHOLD / MODE_HEADHELD gate, three WAITSWITCH_DWN (two stick inputs and a button, the first with no deadline and the other two sharing the routine's own #TIMEOUT), and then a tail where PLYRMODE decides WHOSE MOVE IT IS: MODE_HEADHOLD means the move is mine, MODE_HEADHELD means the same input is a REVERSAL of his, targeting WHOHITME instead of WHOIHIT. tools/wlsmove.py reads the six things that vary -- the three steps, the timeout, the bonus-message index, the animation, whether there is a reversal path, and two extra gates -- into src/generated/smove_hdhold.c, and the runtime builds one monitor descriptor per row around the shared body. Transcribing 42 copies of one routine by hand is exactly what this tree generates instead, and the extraction caught three things a hand copy would very likely have got wrong: SHAWN.ASM:780's shn_flipslam uses a 30-tick window where the other 41 use 60; BRET.ASM:857's hrt_hdhold_combo2 masks only J_DOWN_TOWARD|J_UP_TOWARD on its button step rather than the J_ALL every other row uses; and, worst, these routines are full of COMMENTED-OUT gates -- YOKO.ASM:759 has a GETUP_TIME test commented out for two of Yokozuna's moves and SHAWN.ASM:1538 has CHECK_COMBO_GO commented out for one of Shawn's, and reading the raw text rather than the stripped text counts all three as live and makes three moves refuse in this port that work in the arcade. The 20 still missing are refused on purpose and in four named groups: the 6 charge monitors (a held button, no sequence), the 8 grab_toss_air (two FACE24 macros behind a distance test, so a four-way animation choice the row cannot hold), und_spirit_pull/push in SPECIAL.ASM, and four one-offs. SINCE: the gap is closed -- all 65 distinct monitors are translated, 60 of them read out of the source by tools/wlsmove.py and five written by hand -- and closing it found that four of the forty-two head-hold rows had been read BACKWARDS. The old reader decided a routine was a head-hold monitor by looking for the strings MODE_HEADHOLD and MODE_HEADHELD in its body. Both gates contain both names; what separates them is the DIRECTION of the branch. `cmpi MODE_HEADHOLD,a0 / jrz #cont` enters the sequence on a head hold, and `cmpi MODE_HEADHOLD,a0 / jrz #lp0` goes back to the top -- the move is unavailable while anyone has one. rzr_sliding_rug, shn_sliding_kicktoss and the Undertaker's two spirit moves are the second kind, and were gated on the exact opposite of their real condition. The reader now simulates the gate's branches per mode rather than matching on names. Three more readings were wrong for their own reasons. IMMOBILIZE_TIME was baked in at 15 for every row, and 23 of the 40 are not 15: seventeen say 15, four say 32, one each say 30 and 25, and on seventeen -- every combo move -- the `movk 15,a14 / move a14,*a0(IMMOBILIZE_TIME)` pair is COMMENTED OUT and the move pins nobody at all. The gate is not both modes on every row either: fifteen combo moves are written `cmpi MODE_HEADHOLD,a0 / jrnz #lp0` and belong to the holder alone, so a wrestler whose head is held should never even arm them. And of the twenty-five that do admit him, he has THREE possible answers rather than two -- 23 reverse (DO_REVERSAL, targeting WHOHITME), dnk_hdhold_buzz's tail tests MODE_HEADHOLD and refuses him, and yok_salt_throw tests nothing after the sequence and gives him the same move, which the old reversal-or-refuse model turned into a refusal. SMRTTGT is a column too: rzr_hdhold_combo1, rzr_hdhold_combo2, dnk_hdhold_buzz and yok_salt_throw call it on neither path and aim at nobody, where the port aimed all four at the nearest wrestler. Two of the twenty 'refusals' turned out not to be refusals at all but a body-boundary bug: shn_hdhold_butts and bam_hdhold_pogo are ordinary head-hold monitors, and the `#CHARGE_TIME .equ SM_USRW1` belonging to the CHARGE monitor defined after each of them sits before its own label and so landed at the end of theirs. A third was a real name collision in the source: SPECIAL.ASM:1536 defines a global und_spirit_pull -- the spirit object UNDSEQ4.ASM's animation creates -- and TAKER.ASM:1092 defines a local one, the stick monitor, and `.long und_spirit_pull` inside TAKER.ASM's own smove table binds to the local. Taking the first definition in link order read the wrong routine entirely. The eighteen genuinely new ones are three more families plus two one-offs. CHARGE (6): no input sequence at all -- hold one button, count the ticks on the MONITOR's own process rather than the wrestler's, and on release, if the count reached 100, run a guard list and fire. The counter is incremented BEFORE the button is read, so the tick the button comes up on counts. GRAB_TOSS_AIR (8): three switch steps and then a two-way choice -- an opponent in either air mode, or mid-AT_LEAPING attack, is caught wherever he is, and anyone else has to be inside a per-wrestler CLOSEST_DIST threshold (68h, 6ch or 70h). Five pick each animation with FACE24 and three name it outright, and Lex's FACE24 lines are commented out, so reading raw text gives him a facing pair he does not have. FREE (6): the head-hold shape with the gate taken off. What all three share is a LIST OF REFUSALS at the end, and that list is what varies most, so it is extracted as data -- an instruction the reader does not recognise refuses the whole routine rather than being dropped, because a test that quietly failed to translate is a move that fires here and would not in the arcade. The two written by hand have a THIRD outcome and nothing shared to parametrise: shn_flipslam ("Can do from head hold also!", says the source) does the same animation from a neutral stance with no target, no bonus and nobody pinned, and shn_swirl_speedkick turns into an entirely different move -- a flying knee with DELAY_METER, SPCDMG and SETMODE INAIR -- when he is holding a head, while its reversal path falls THROUGH into the slam because the `jruc #is_reversal` after DO_REVERSAL is commented out. Two things the runtime gained with them: the trailing SLEEP every one of these routines runs before looping (20 ticks mostly, 120 on the spirit moves, TSEC*3 on Bam Bam's neckbreaker), which was not modelled at all and without which a held input re-fires the move every tick; and the victim's IMMOBILIZE_TIME, which the monitors reported and match.c never applied. What is still NOT here: the BONUS_MESS message objects and DO_REVERSAL_MESS, which are AWARD.ASM display; the WRSND calls; and the commented-out OBJ_XVEL writes in shn_swirl_speedkick's knee path, which are commented out in the source too.

between_round_reset.note: A decided round was a dead end. wm/arcade/wm_arcade_round.h had been saying so outright -- "this port has no round-2 restart at all, so match_winner becoming nonzero is currently a dead end" -- and it was worse than that: the score moved and nothing else did, so the match kept ticking with both wrestlers frozen where they fell and round_state.decided stuck true, which meant no further round could ever be called. LIFEBAR.ASM:3098's WRESTLERS_RESET block is what should happen instead, and it is now translated and wired (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_round_reset.h). WRESTLE.ASM:2630 reset_for_round: the per-side starting table read out of the source (three rows a side of X, Z and facing, team 1 based at Z 1127 and team 2 at 1103) plus the rule that picks the row -- "the number of teammates with PLYRNUM's lower than ours", counted by walking the process list and stopping at yourself -- then GROUND_Y, the veladd clamp the source inlines so a wrestler starts standing ON the mat rather than falling to it, the facings, the mode and velocity clears, the 14*60 DELAY_METER ("Don't allow meters for the first x seconds of round"), and the FOOT_PCNT stamp, which is a WORD store and truncates. One line in it is easy to get exactly backwards: `clr INRING` puts a wrestler INSIDE the ring, and this port keeps in_ring as an ordinary boolean, so it is SET here -- the opposite spelling would start every round with both men counted out. WRESTLE.ASM:2797 reset_for_round2: IMMOBILIZE_TIME 30, the per-round field clears, PLYR.EQU:443's SF_RESET_MASK (exactly TEMP_PAL and DID_BUCKOFF survive a round; PINNED, DID_PIN, KOD, ZOMBIE, PINABLE and GUY_UP all go), and the PTIME of 1 the source sets "just in case they were KO'd last round", which is what lets the loser fight the next one. Three more routines from the same block came with it. WRESTLE.ASM:6688 init_scroller -- the camera does NOT start at the origin, it starts at RING_X_CENTER-200 with a negative Y ([0ffe5h,0], or [0ffe9h,0] when NUM_OPPS is exactly 2), and leaving it at zero put the ring off the right of the first frame. WRESTLE.ASM:3003 update_links, five instructions that drop an ATTACH_PROC which is not pointing back at you, now run once a tick per wrestler as the source runs it -- without it a puppet can be dragged around by somebody who has already let go. And WRESTLE.ASM:1359 show_most_damage's decision half, which is worth stating because the answer surprises: it SKIPS DRONES and does not put their damage in the total either, so a human fighting a drone did 100% of "the damage" however hard the drone hit him, and a tie goes to player 2. WRESTLE2.ASM contributed loser_snd (two humans only, the LOSER's old streak found by turning the winner's index inside out with `NOT / ANDI 3 / DEC`, and a RNDRNG0(2) pick from the three lines the source left uncommented) and maybe_do_flashes' two gates. WHEN it runs matters as much as what it does. The source reaches WRESTLERS_RESET from deep inside announce_rnd_winner -- past `#fini_wait`, the buckoff window, the victory sound, CALL_MATCH_OVER, the dufus messages and a 105-tick button wait -- and this port models almost none of that presentation, so it cannot reproduce the delay honestly. What it does reproduce is the one gate that changes behaviour rather than timing: LIFEBAR.ASM:2649's `#fini_wait`, where the announcement (and therefore everything downstream of it) polls while @in_finish_move is set. Running the reset on the deciding tick instead was tried first and is wrong twice over -- it wiped the Undertaker's coffin sequence half-way through, for the round that sequence had just won, and it cleared round_state.decided on the same tick it was set, which is an observable two existing tests were reading. So the reset is OWED on the deciding tick and run at the top of a later one, once no finishing move is in progress. What is NOT translated is everything around the reset that draws or sounds: CLEAR_SPEECH_REPEAT, the round-2/round-3 music, CLOSE_VERT_SCREEN_LINE and the wipe, the text plates, the clock palette, the meters and INIT_SKIRTS. With this, WRESTLE2.ASM has no open routines left and WRESTLE.ASM has two. The eighteen that closed are the arcade's own scaffolding -- game_loop and wrestler_main (the cooperative scheduler wm_match_tick replaced, checked against reset_for_round2's own trailing `reset_start2` block, which is that per-tick pipeline written out straight), game_interrupt, init_prog, WARMSET, CLEAR_PROCESSES, set_process_ptr and its twin, change_image, DO_SET_IMAGES, direction_test, choose_pal, choose_buddies and wrestler_counter -- each ledgered with the source line and the reason, not a shrug. The two still open are plyr_strtb1 and plyr_strtb2, the mid-match buy-in: this port has no credit or start handler for them to be part of, so they stay counted rather than being pointed at a symbol that does not exist. direction_test is worth one line of its own, because the first attempt got it wrong: it was ledgered `dead` and a source-tool test refused that, correctly -- `dead` means literally zero references and it has one, its own `CREATE 0,direction_test` carrying the comment "temp!!!!!!!!!!!" and sitting inside the `.if 0` that wraps the routine's first half. Nothing built can reach it, but the count is 1.

end_of_match.note: LIFEBAR.ASM:2852 DO_WAIT. A finished match was a dead end the same way a decided round was before the last change: wm_arcade_match_score_award_round set match_winner and nothing took over, so the match kept ticking with two wrestlers standing in a ring that had already been won. Translated as phases on the match (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_match_end.h), with the source's own sleeps -- SLEEPK 20, a second, the 15/10/20 between the three end-of-round graphics, and three seconds -- so it takes the several hundred ticks it should rather than collapsing to one. WRESTLE.ASM:1445 increment_wincount came with it and was ledgered WRONG: it was pointed at wm_arcade_match_score_award_round and described as "credit a round to a side", which is not what it does. It is the win-STREAK bookkeeping: save both streaks to p1oldwinstreak / p2oldwinstreak FIRST (that pair is what WRESTLE2.ASM's loser_snd reads to tell a broken streak from no streak, so the copy has to precede the update), AND match_winner with PSTATUS so a player who is not in the game cannot have won, then increment each side's streak or CLEAR it to zero -- the increment is computed before the test and discarded on a loss, which is why losing resets rather than decrements. Three more decisions in the same path: the end-of-round graphic index, which is the round NUMBER (rounds played less one) and not the winner, pinned to 2 once anyone has two; the mk3-tip rule, whose structure is not the obvious one -- p2's streak is looked at ONLY when p1's is zero, and a streak that is not a multiple of 25 falls THROUGH to the every-100-matches test rather than giving up; and DO_RIGHT_MUSIC's `#wrestler_tunes .word 5,2,1,7,6,4,8,0,3`, the winner's own theme by WRESTLERNUM. The five award routines the path calls -- is_it_a_really_quick_win, give_award_if_opponent_is_human, check_for_award_for_big_comeback, accumulate_awards and check_for_award_for_winstreak -- were all already translated and had never been called by anything; this is the call site they lacked. Two of them decline for a visible reason rather than being skipped: the quick-win award reads @match_time, which this port has no round clock to fill in, and the comeback award is armed elsewhere and nothing arms it yet. Not translated: replace_wins and the win-count text, the three CREATE_END_ROUND_* graphics, the award bar (create_end_rnd_awards) and its @award_ok_to_die poll, show_mk3_tip itself, and the button presses that cut the two waits short.

streamed_roster_art.note: The translated match reaches a screen. src/platform/n64/main.c's render_source_match drives off wm_match_build_draw_list -- the translated wm/match_display.h, with its obj_yzsort order, its shadow/body/torso layers and its ODXOFF/ODYOFF anchors -- and off wm_match_state::scroll.worldtlx/y, the translated WRESTLE2.ASM:1681 camera. The old rectangle-and-demo-fighter harness that used to stand in for it is still in the file but is marked unused and nothing calls it. So the chain is whole: the animation VM's current frame for each actor, through the draw list, through a DragonFS sprite, to the RDP. src/platform/n64/streamed_character_art.c is the last link: an 8-slot LRU over rom:/wrestlers/<num>/<frame>.bin, so the art stays in ROM and only what is on screen is resident. tools/stream_roster_assets.py emits it from the SAME frame set the port already generates geometry for, and refuses outright if any frame has no .LOD owner. MEASURED, which is the point of looking: 5,126 frames, 8 wrestlers, 39,987,436 bytes -- 38.1 MiB of wrestler art alone, before backgrounds, audio and code. That needs a 64 Mbit-class cartridge and it is worth having the number written down rather than an estimate. 2.5 MiB of it was pure duplication: every frame carried its own 512-byte 256-colour TLUT, and the whole roster has only 23 distinct palettes between its 5,126 frames (Bret 619 frames and two palettes; the Undertaker 608 and seven). The palettes are now written once each as pN.pal and each frame carries a four-byte header naming its own, which takes the payload to 37,395,204 bytes -- 2,592,232 bytes back, with no loss of anything. All 5,126 emitted files were checked to round-trip: magic, a palette index that resolves to a file that exists, and a pixel count that matches the frame's generated geometry exactly. One thing the look found that was not about assets at all: tools/n64_link_check.py deliberately skips src/platform/n64 because it "genuinely needs libdragon headers", so in a checkout without libdragon -- which is this container and every CI host here -- the platform layer was compiled by NOTHING. Rewriting the frame loader with no build behind it is not acceptable, so tests/host_shims/libdragon.h declares the one entry point that loader really uses and tools/n64_platform_check.py type-checks it with -Wall -Wextra. It is not a ROM build and does not pretend to be; it catches the class of thing an unverified edit gets wrong. main.c is deliberately NOT covered: it pulls in rdpq, display, controller and audio, and a shim big enough for that would be a fake libdragon rather than a check.

round_clock.note: WRESTLE2.ASM:4098 match_timer's clock, and LIFEBAR.ASM:5149 set_winner's #tmout branch. A round could only end by knockout or pin, so a match where neither happened never finished -- and five other routines already translated in this tree were reading @match_time and getting a permanent zero: ANIM.ASM:73 animate_wrestler stops animating entirely at zero, WRESTLE.ASM:2541 releases a wrestler's GETUP_TIME at zero, AWARD.ASM:996 is_it_a_really_quick_win scores the win by what is left on it (so every win scored zero and that award could never fire), LIFEBAR.ASM's set_winner has a whole branch for it, and the main loop at WRESTLE.ASM:2102 ends the round on it. Translated (wm/arcade/wm_arcade_match_clock.h): the 99/99/0 init; the `callr #create_timer / SLEEP TSEC*2` the routine opens with, so a match does not start losing time on the bell; the rate, which is #timer_table[ADJSPEED-1] with the royal-rumble/1-on-3 two-thirds (`movi >AAAA / mpyu / srl 16`) and the final-match halving, both of which the rumble takes, which is how the source's own "1/3 speed" comment comes out right; #dec_timer; the #loop gate; WRESTLE.ASM:2115's attract wraparound; WRESTLE.ASM:2657's between-round reset; and the #tmout rule. @match_time is NOT a seconds counter and reading it as one gets the feel of the round wrong. It is three WORDS -- `BSSX match_time, 16*3`, and the comment beside it gives the order as frac, 1's, 10's -- of which only two are digits. The third is a 16-bit fraction with the rate subtracted from it every tick, and the clock moves one unit each time that BORROWS. At the factory-default rate of 1500 that is 4282 ticks for the whole 99, about 81 seconds at DISPLAY.EQU:46's 53 Hz. The source's own comment on that table row says 53.6 seconds and the arithmetic does not produce it; the `.asg 1500,BASETM ;2100 ;16` line shows BASETM was lowered from 2100 and the comments beside it were not updated. The shipped arithmetic is what is transcribed. Two details in #loop are easy to miss and both change play. The clock does NOT run while either side is wiped out (`get_live_bits / cmpi 3,a3 / jrne #1tmded`), so the five-second pin window after a knockout does not eat into the round. And in attract mode the clock never ends anything: `move @PSTATUS,a14 / jrnz #norm` rolls it back to 99 and the demo keeps going. The expiry rule is the source's own summary of it: award the round to the side with the highest AVERAGE life remaining -- a dead wrestler is counted, with the zero he has, rather than left out -- tie-broken by whoever landed a hit most recently (LAST_HIT_TIME is stamped on the ATTACKER), and if nobody has landed a blow at all it returns -1 and awards the round to nobody, which is what the source does rather than picking someone. Not translated, and all of it drawing: update_timer's two digit objects and the palette that turns them red at ten; LIFEBAR.ASM:4876 CREATE_TIMEOUT, the TIME OUT graphic and its flash animation; and the warning sound itself -- #dec_timer's `movk 10,a0 / calla triple_sound` is surfaced as a one-tick flag on the match rather than played, because nothing in this port plays a sound and the crowd channel beside it is the crowd's. The is_8_on_1/royal_rumble override that hands a timed-out round to the CPU outright is also absent: this port has no team system for it to read.

post_match_flow.note: WRESTLE.ASM:1116, the code after `JSRP start_match` -- and the source's own comment on it is the specification: "The only time we return from start_match is when the match is over and the game must goto: 1. Buy-in screen for 1 or 2 player games. 2. Ladder screen for the next matchup. 3. Finale screens." app.c had no such return at all. WM_APP_MODE_MATCH was terminal: a match that finished left the game ticking a decided match for ever, which is the same dead end a decided ROUND was before the between-round reset and a finished MATCH was before DO_WAIT -- the third and last link in that chain. The hinge is @match_over. WRESTLE.ASM:221 declares it "0=not over, !0=over"; LIFEBAR.ASM:2985's `MOVK 2,A0 / move a0,@match_over` is the last thing DO_WAIT does before it dies; and WRESTLE.ASM:2087's main loop polls it and RETPs out of game_loop, which is how the arcade leaves a match. wm_match_tick now sets it and wm_app_tick reads it. The branch is `move @PSTATUS,a0 / move @match_winner,a1 / andn a1,a0 / jrnz #go_buyin` -- did a human LOSE. A human who WON goes straight back to the pregame and the next rung of the ladder with NO select screen (`jruc do_pregame`), which is the arcade's "keep playing". A human who lost gets `#go_buyin`: the CPU won, so match_winner is cleared and CURRENT_LADDER steps BACK a rung -- the source says why in its own comment, "because NEXT_IN_LADDER automatically increments it" -- and then SELECT.ASM's buyin_select. That last one needed nothing written: wm/select_continue.h has been a complete translation of it for a long time, app.c called wm_select_continue_init on it at boot, and nothing ever reached it. Closing the loop exposed a real bug that could not bite while a match was a dead end: src/core/pregame.c's enter_progress called INIT_LADDER_TABLE. The source does not -- it calls it once per GAME, from ATTRACT.ASM:595 and SELECT.ASM's GAME_BEATEN, while PROGRESS.ASM:2689's PUT_UP_PROGRESS does NEXT_IN_LADDER once per MATCH. Rebuilding the table on every pregame put the player back on rung zero, so the moment a second match became reachable he would have fought the first opponent for ever. One platform boundary is drawn deliberately and is not the arcade's: in the cabinet a COIN buys in (`#buyin: PSTATUS bit became active`) and Start only resets the countdown. A console has no coin door, so Start IS the buy-in here -- the same boundary app.c already draws for player two joining the select screen -- and it is read as an edge so a Start carried over from the match does not spend itself. The countdown still runs and letting it reach zero still ends the game. Not translated: AUD_TOTALGAMES and the rest of postgame_audits (no audit store here); the royal-rumble branch at #finished_rumble and everything under it; pin_speed_in_case's high-score entry for the loser; is_final_match's jump to finished_game and the finale screens; loser_snd, which is a sound this port does not play; and LIFEBAR.ASM's do_game_over, still open -- a declined continue goes straight back to attract the way a finished demo does, rather than through a game-over screen that does not exist yet. SINCE: SELECT.ASM:1190 do_game_over, which a declined continue used to skip straight past on its way to attract. On entry the ladder is rebuilt (";kill the ladder", says the source's own comment on its INIT_LADDER_TABLE) and FADE_MASTER_VOL is started; then four seconds of GAME OVER with the volume ramping down under it -- 100 ticks against 4*53, so it reaches silence well before the screen goes. Afterwards the board is silenced, ADJVOLUME is read back and set_volume restores it (or attract would start muted for the rest of the machine's life), both players' icon totals are cleared, and it jumps to attract. The fade's arithmetic is kept exactly: the source builds the step as `volume << 16 / ticks` and subtracts it from a 16.16 accumulator, and doing it in integers instead lands short. Still display: display_blank, WIPEOUT, GENERIC_DISPLAY, the two JAM_STR plates that put GAME and OVER on the screen, and UNIT_CLR.

compressed_text.note: AWARD.ASM:3056 decompress_string, and the text nobody in this port had ever read. Eleven instructions: `setf 6,0,0`, then each six-bit field plus 1Fh is a character and a zero field ends the string. So the alphabet is 0x20-0x5F exactly -- uppercase ASCII and punctuation, nothing else -- packed four characters into every three bytes, least significant bits first. That is the whole compressor and it buys about a quarter. What it unpacks is real content: the two Mortal Kombat 3 tips WrestleMania hides behind a win streak, with the six-icon button code each one tells you to enter, and the eight wrestlers' ending stories -- 1,889 lines of source across BAMST.H, BRETST.H, DOINKST.H, LEXST.H, RAZORST.H, SHAWNST.H, TAKERST.H and YOKOST.H, none of it legible without running the decompressor. 224 blobs, 218 distinct story lines reached by 245 references, because Adam Bomb is given Doink's stories -- the same hand-me-down the animation dispatch tables make for him. The extraction checks itself. Whatever tool Midway compressed these with left the plaintext in a comment beside every blob, so tools/wlstorytext.py decodes the bytes and compares, refusing on any mismatch. 224 known answers, all of which agreed -- the decompressor is verified rather than asserted. The rest of AWARD.ASM's open routines were triaged rather than translated, and that took the file from 63 open to 3. Thirty-two of them were never routines at all: the MK3 tip strings, the twelve icon object records, and the pointer tables over them, all now ledgered `data` and most of them extracted. Thirty-one are the display half -- the icon bars, the sparkle, the dufus message boxes, the tip screen's coin and smoke -- ledgered `display` with what each one draws, because the award CONDITIONS were already translated in wm/award.h and run on the real call sites; it is only the showing of them that is missing. suspend_game and suspend_all are `process`: they freeze the arcade's cooperative process list, and there is no such list here to freeze. Not translated: the drawing, and show_mk3_tip's own screen -- the tips and their codes are extracted and readable, but nothing puts them up.

background_scroller.note: BAKGND.ASM's background scroller: BGND_UD1 (:358), bgnd_scanmod (:397), bgnd_addmod (:457), bgnd_get1stx (:182) and bgnd_delnonvis (:794), over the module data tools/wlbgnd.py reads out of BGNDTBL.ASM. scroll_world had been translated for a long time and moved the camera over nothing. This is what it moves over. A background is a MODULE of blocks placed at a world position, and WRESTLE.ASM:1615 hands a match exactly one: `movi ring_mod,a0 / move a0,@BAKMODS,L`, naming ringBMOD at (105,-450) -- 1972x868, 211 blocks. Every refresh deletes the blocks that have scrolled off and adds the ones that have scrolled on, keeping a residency bit per block (BAKBITS) so each one is added once and deleted once. What comes out here is that SET plus its two edges, for a renderer to act on; the object allocation and the DMA are not translated. src/generated/bmod_tables.c already carried block words for five FRONTEND modules through the asset pipeline, but not the ring, and no header sizes at all -- so a new source-data reader was written rather than the asset path disturbed. Three things in the routine are easy to lose and all three are load bearing. THE BLOCKS ARE SORTED BY X, and the scan exploits it twice: a binary search picks the starting block, and once a block's left edge is past the display's the scan drops into a cheaper test and stops at the first block past the right edge. Walking all 211 would give the same answer and miss the routine's point, and a test checks the sortedness the whole thing rests on. A BLOCK CARRIES NO SIZE -- its record has a palette, flags, Z, X, Y and an index into the module's header table, where the width and height live, and that indirection is exactly why the two scan phases differ. And ADDING AND DELETING DO NOT USE THE SAME TEST: adding needs X < right and Y < bottom, deleting keeps on X <= right and Y <= bottom, so a block exactly on the edge is not added but is not deleted either once it is there. That asymmetry is in the shipped code and is reproduced rather than tidied; flattening it would make edge blocks flicker as the camera creeps. The scan is checked against a brute-force sweep over all 211 blocks at 53 camera positions, and bgnd_get1stx against a linear search at 370 targets, so the two optimisations are verified rather than trusted. One reading worth recording: get1stx returns a bare 0 for "not found", which is also a valid block index. This port returns the block COUNT instead, because a caller that read the source's 0 as an index would start from the left of the world every frame. Not translated: bgnd_addblk's object allocation and DMA control word (the ordering rule it uses is already wm/bmod.h's wm_bmod_draw_before), and BGNDHGHT, the background-height query used by the ring-out code. One note on the ledger: bgnd_scanmod, bgnd_delnonvis and bgnd_get1stx needed no entry at all -- the port's functions carry their names, so the coverage tool resolves them on its own, and a hand-written entry beside a name that already resolves is only able to go stale. The source-tool test refuses one.

ending_story.note: STORIES.ASM print_story and show_wrestler_end_story, translated in wm/arcade/wm_arcade_story.h. The 245 story lines had been unpacked and then had nothing to show them; this is the sequencing. print_story pages twelve lines at a time (y=90 stepping 12 while below 230), holds a full page for SLEEP TSEC*5 and then up to TSEC*15 with a button skip, erases and turns the page. Its terminator test is at the TOP of the page loop and jumps past both waits, so a final page that is not exactly twelve lines gets no hold of its own -- it is held instead by show_wrestler_end_story's own TSEC*15 wait after JSRP print_story, which is why the two are translated together. show_wrestler_end_story adds which_player[PSTATUS>>1], the wrestler-7 bail (slot 7's logo entry in w_logos is a literal 0), the 30-tick fade, and the mugshot/logo/belt placement constants. The three BEGINOBJ calls are the display layer's and are flagged per-tick rather than faked; only story zero of each wrestler is ever shown, which is what `move *a1,a1,L` twice does.

victory_fireworks.note: FIREWORK.ASM, translated in wm/arcade/wm_arcade_firework.h with tools/wlfirework.py emitting src/generated/firework_tables.c. Nine of the file's twenty-three routines are SUBRP data tables and are read out rather than retyped: the 61-waypoint figure-of-eight panning_points, the flare and explosion image lists, the five palettes, and the three congratulations message sets -- each of which pairs a JAM_STR placement table with a string table positionally, where only the placement table is terminated, so the reader checks the lengths agree. The twenty-two flare coordinates are not written as a table at all (do_fireworks loads them into a9 one at a time, twelve of them from a dsjs loop), so the reader runs those four instructions instead of having the numbers retyped. The camera is fully translated: calc_dxdy's signed divide, move_camera, check_camera_position's three-pixel stop per axis, and pan_around's segment loop including the text going up exactly once and the flight home to @final_x/@final_y. firework_flare and animate_fwexp are translated as tick machines, including that #flare_anim2 is a label five images INSIDE #flare_anim rather than a table of its own, and that the fizzle walks five images backwards with a pre-decrement. do_fireworks itself is partial: knockout_drones, the flare positions, the explosion budget and the pan are here; its twenty KIL1C and ten obj_del1c calls are against process and object IDs this port does not have and are not invented. Two findings worth recording: pan_around loads `movk 15,a10` commented 'Number of ticks for this move' and calc_dxdy never reads a10, so the dead 15 is not what flies the camera -- the table's own first column is; and AUDIT.ASM's form_crc32, met while triaging the same group, is not a CRC32 at all but an xor-and-rotate-left-one rolling checksum.

shared_object_utilities.note: wm/arcade/wm_arcade_objutil.h. Fifty-six routines across MAIN, DISPLAY, UTIL, MENU, DIAG, MPROC, AUDIT, TEST and SCREEN were sitting open on the assumption that they all talk to the coin door, the PIC or the DMA. Most of them do and are now individually ledgered as such, each with what it actually touches. Six are not hardware at all and are translated: GETCPNT (object centre, including why `srl 1` on the packed size needs the 7fff mask in the low word and why the 7fff in the high word is dead after a logical shift), obj_find (the masked OID walk, where the mask names the bits to IGNORE), obj_addworldxy, anipt_getxy (the horizontal-flip attach point, decremented in whole pixels before the shift), vol_to_ht, and form_crc32 -- which is not a CRC32: it is xor-and-rotate-left-one over the adjustment block, with no polynomial and no table, and the test says so. Three more resolved to work already done: process_init and process_dispatch are wm_scheduler_init / wm_scheduler_step, IKIL1C is one instruction in front of IKILALLN, and DRKTRPLTP is not a routine at all but a 32-word darkened palette. Triaging the group also turned up a tooling bug: tools/port_coverage.py filtered the ledger's own _README by testing for a leading underscore, which silently dropped any entry for the five real routines whose names start with one (_GetTime, _AlarmClock, _get_time, _set_time, _aquire_time) -- the ledger said one thing and the report said another with nothing to show they disagreed. It filters on the shape now and refuses anything that is neither an entry nor the README.

hiscore_colour_cyclers.note: UTIL.ASM:1174 CYCLE_TABLE, translated in wm/arcade/wm_arcade_colcyc.h with tools/wlcolcyc.py emitting src/generated/colcyc_tables.c. HSTD.ASM's hscore_colcyc and hscore_colcyc2 are six instructions each that load the same four arguments -- colour 10, seven colours, every three ticks -- and CREATE the shared cycler, so the cycler is the routine and the two are its arguments. Two things the source does not write down: the cycle restarts when the word it lands on is negative OR equal to the table's FIRST word, so the period is the distance to the next repeat of word zero (63 of 78 in both tables) and the 15-word tail exists only so the seven-colour window can be read from the last position; and the loop re-reads the palette record before every write and DIEs if it changed, which is what stops a cycler that outlived its page from writing into whatever got the slot next. The reader works the period out and refuses a table where word zero never repeats. Also corrected in this pass: a sleep tick is a whole tick, and the instruction after a SLEEP runs on the tick the process RESUMES -- an off-by-one that had put the fireworks' congratulations text up a tick early and had the flare's first animation frame share a tick with the object's creation.

lifebar_z_flip.note: LIFEBAR.ASM:4039 SHIFT_BARS_IN_Z, translated in wm/arcade/wm_arcade_lifebar.h. A four-tick poll of WORLDTLY against ZFLIP_POS_VAR with one flag of hysteresis, pushing every object in the [bak_z, name_z] band 1800h forward so the top rope cannot draw over the life bars when the camera rises, and back when it drops. Two things worth recording. The threshold is a variable and the end of a round sets it to ZFLIP_FOR_SURE (0F0F00000h) -- a value no camera position can be below -- which is how the bars are forced forward for the winner's announcement without a second code path. And LAST_FLIP is not what keeps the arithmetic correct: the band moves with the shift (SHIFT_BARS_BACK tests the forward band offset by the shift), so a repeated shift finds nothing in range and is already a no-op; what the flag saves is walking the whole object list every fourth tick to discover that. SLOOP 4 puts the body on every fourth tick, the tick it runs on being the first of the four.

lifebar_rewire.note: LIFEBAR.ASM:880 rewire_monitor, translated in wm/arcade/wm_arcade_lifebar.h. It decides which wrestler the second life bar is showing, and it is three unrelated loops sharing a name and an entry point. Normal: follow the human's CLOSEST_NUM, debounced by TSEC/2 so the bar does not flicker between two drones taking turns -- and the debounce is waived when the wrestler currently SHOWN is dead, not when the new one is, which is the distinction the source's comment draws and the easy one to get backwards. Rumble: alternate between a pair, holding each for TSEC*4/10 POLLS (a8 is decremented once per SLOOP 10, so that is forty polls and not forty ticks), swapping early when the one on display dies, and refusing to swap onto a dead one -- so with both dead the bar keeps showing a corpse rather than blanking. Buddy: two independent displays, each following its human or, if he is dead, his partner's drone, and both can rewire in the same pass, which is why the port reports a list of rewire_meter calls per tick rather than a flag. rewire_meter itself rebuilds the meter graphics and is the display layer's.

start_button.note: WRESTLE.ASM:663 plyr_strtb1 / plyr_strtb2, translated in wm/arcade/wm_arcade_plyr_start.h. Two entry points with one body -- the only difference between the players is the bit a8 holds -- and it is how a second player joins a game in progress as well as how the first one starts. Three guards (a negative GAMSTATE is the diagnostic menu, INPARTY is the winner's party, and a PSTATUS bit already set means he is in), then the per-player wipe, then the credit. The order is the finding: the wipe happens BEFORE CR_STRTP, so a player turned away for want of a coin has already lost his win streak, his entered initials, his process pointer and his accumulated pin time. One field survives it -- a NEGATIVE winstreakd is left alone by `move *a4,a0 / jrn #a4ok`. The exit is a seven-way branch on GAMSTATE with two LOCKUPs, which the port reports as an outcome rather than halting.

select_pin_speed_clock.note: SELECT.ASM:533 work_out_match_time and calc_match_time_2, translated in wm/arcade/wm_arcade_string.h alongside BCDBIN, which they need and which the port did not have. The routine answers two things: the match clock in the 0xIIFF form the caller's own comment describes, and the round's tick span in hundredths of a second. The second is where it goes wrong. `movi (100<<8)/55` converts at FIFTY-FIVE ticks per second while DISPLAY.EQU:46 says TSEC is 53 and everything else in the game counts in 53s, so every pin time the high score table has ever held is about 3.6% short of the time the player took -- 3.6% plus another 0.1% for the assembler truncating (100<<8)/55 to 465. This is translated as written, and the test asserts the wrong answer on purpose: a pin time that does not match the arcade's is a different game.

open_routine_ledger.note: Every one of the 2534 routines tools/port_coverage.py enumerates now has an answer: 1969 implemented, 160 renamed, 128 display, 68 hardware, 53 data, 37 dead, 22 process, 20 partial, 13 inlined, 64 unassembled. Nothing is left as 'unknown' or 'cited'. Read that as a statement about the LEDGER and not about the port being finished: 128 display and 68 hardware entries are routines this port deliberately does not carry, and each one now says what it touches and why rather than sitting unexamined. What reaching zero buys is that the next regression has nowhere to hide -- a routine that stops resolving becomes open again, and the source-tool tests refuse a ledger entry that names a routine the automatic pass already resolves, one that claims a port symbol that does not exist, or a 'dead' entry with any reference at all. That last guard earned its keep during this pass: three fields I named after the source routines they stood for (match_timer, reset_dufus_msgs, clear_icon_total) made those routines resolve by accident, and the test caught all three.
